query: For high-entropy-alloy protective coatings in wear-resistant applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their wear performance and why? Define a controlled change that would distinguish the hypothesis from a baseline, the directional observations expected if it is correct, the range over which it should hold, the prior evidence that supports it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing the content of a reactive element (e.g., Cr or Al) in a high-entropy alloy protective coating promotes the formation of a stable, nano‐scale tribo‐layer during sliding contact, thereby reducing wear rates under ambient conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloy protective coatings with a baseline reactive element content (e.g., standard weight % of Cr or Al) applied on a substrate.
generation.intervention: Systematically adjust (increase or decrease by a few weight %) the reactive element content in the HEA composition.
generation.conditions: Pin‐on‐disk wear testing performed at ambient conditions (room temperature, ~50% relative humidity) with standard sliding speeds (up to ~1 m/s) and controlled applied loads, combined with in situ surface analysis (using XPS and TEM).
generation.structural_mediator: A nano‐scale tribo‐layer that forms on the coating surface during wear.
generation.mechanism: An increased reactive element content enhances the chemical reactivity at the sliding interface, leading to more rapid and stable formation of a protective tribo‐layer (e.g., oxide or similar compound), which reduces friction and wear by acting as a self‐healing barrier during the wear process.
generation.predicted_outcome: Coatings with increased reactive element content will show a more continuous and stable tribo‐layer, lower wear volume, and a reduced coefficient of friction compared to the baseline composition. Conversely, coatings with reduced reactive element content will show less effective tribo‐layer formation and higher wear rates.
generation.baseline: The HEA coating with the standard reactive element composition exhibits a less developed tribo‐layer and correspondingly higher wear rate.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold for variations within a few weight % change in reactive element content and under ambient, room‐temperature wear conditions. Its applicability at very high temperatures or for extreme mechanical loads remains untested.
generation.uncertainty: The exact chemical composition and microstructural characteristics of the tribo‐layer, as well as potential interference from other alloying elements or environmental factors, introduce uncertainty in the magnitude of the wear reduction and may require further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of HEA protective coatings on substrates with systematically varied reactive element (e.g., Cr or Al) content (baseline, +a few weight %, -a few weight %). Subject each to standardized pin-on-disk wear tests under identical ambient conditions, while performing in situ surface analyses (XPS and TEM) to monitor tal layer formation.
measurements: Characterization and continuity of the tribo‐layer via XPS and TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no trend is observed between increased reactive element content and improved tribo‐layer formation (i.e., no significant decrease in wear rate or friction coefficient) compared to the baseline, or if variations in composition do not lead to systematic changes in the tribo‐layer characteristics, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: While the AlCoFeNi high entropy alloy exhibits a single ordered B2 phase at high temperature, both the substitution of ferromagnetic Co with antiferromagnetic Cr, and lower annealing temperatures lead to a tendency for this system to decompose into a two-phase mixture of ordered B2 and disordered BCC solid solution. The length scale of this decomposition is determined by the combination of composition and annealing temperature, as demonstrated in this investigation by comparing and contrasting AlCoFeNi with the AlCo 0.5 Cr 0.5 FeNi alloy. The resulting phase stability has been rationalized based on solution thermodynamic predictions. Additionally, it is shown that replacement of Co by Cr in the AlCoFeNi alloy resulted in a substantial reduction in saturation magnetization and increase in coercivity. The microhardness is also strongly influenced by the composition and the length scale of B2 + BCC decomposition in these high entropy alloys.

Abstract In this study, the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEAs) is investigated at elevated temperatures. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of inert gas atomised feedstock enables the production of dense bulk material. The microstructure evolution and phase formation are analysed. The high cooling rate in the atomisation process results in spherical powder with a microstructure comprising two finely distributed body-centred cubic phases. An additional phase with a complex crystal structure precipitates during SPS processing, while no coarsening of microstructural features occurs. The wear resistance under reciprocating wear conditions increases at elevated temperatures due to the formation of a protective oxide layer under atmospherical conditions. Additionally, the coefficient of friction (COF) slightly decreases with increasing temperature. SPS processing is suitable for the production of HEA bulk material. An increase in the wear resistance at elevated temperature enables high temperature applications of the HEA system AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 . chosen.lever: reactive element content in the HEA composition
chosen.technique: pin‐on‐disk wear testing with in situ tribo‐layer characterization (using XPS and TEM)
chosen.conditions: tests performed under controlled ambient conditions (room temperature, ~50% relative humidity) while systematically varying the content of a reactive element (± a few weight %), across standard sliding speeds (e.g., up to 1 m/s) and loads
chosen.why: This move directly addresses the open question by formulating a mechanistic hypothesis: that wear performance is governed by the formation and stability of a nano‐scale tribo-layer which is highly sensitive to the alloy composition. By deliberately varying the reactive element content, this experiment distinguishes the hypothesis from the baseline state, using standard controlled-variable techniques common in high-entropy alloy wear studies. Expected directional changes (enhanced tribo-layer stability leading to lower wear rates) and the possibility of falsification (i.e., no change in wear performance despite compositional variation) make this approach testable and directly aligned with the niche.
